title: D-DOIT: Training-free Adaptation of Discrete Diffusion via Doob’s h-Transform

paper.title: D-DOIT: Training-free Adaptation of Discrete Diffusion via Doob’s h -Transform
paper.abstract:
Abstract We propose D-DOIT (Discrete Doob-Oriented Inference-time Transformation), a training-free and efficient adaptation method for discrete diffusion models with generic rewards.
D-DOIT formulates adaptation as sampling from a reward-tilted target distribution and realizes this transport through Doob’s h h -transform of the discrete diffusion reverse kernel, using only reward values rather than reward gradients.
Unlike continuous diffusion, masked discrete diffusion samples categorical token-reveal transitions rather than continuous state updates.
D-DOIT derives the corresponding discrete Doob’s h h -transform, which guides sampling by reweighting reverse transition probabilities instead of adding a drift correction.
To make this transformation practical, D-DOIT avoids expensive future rollouts.
At each guided step, D-DOIT samples candidate next states, uses the model prediction head to complete each candidate into a clean sequence, evaluates each completion with the reward oracle, and resamples the next state with probabilities proportional to the rewards.
An optional late-stage best-of- K K refinement further improves sample quality by branching trajectories only near the end of denoising, avoiding the K K -fold cost over the full trajectory.
Empirically, across regulatory DNA design and protein inverse folding benchmarks, D-DOIT outperforms training-free guidance baselines.
It improves enhancer activity and cell-type specificity while preserving sequence naturalness, and achieves the highest success rate in protein inverse folding. Project Page: https://github.com/WeiminWu2000/D-DOIT .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: We propose D-DOIT ( D iscrete D oob- O riented I nference-time T ransformation), a training-free sampler for reward-guided masked discrete diffusion. Discrete diffusion has become a strong generative modeling paradigm for finite-vocabulary data [ 1 , 2 ] . Masked discrete diffusion models are especially attractive for biological sequences because they predict clean tokens from partially masked states and provide tractable categorical reverse kernels [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . These models have recently been used for DNA and protein generation [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] , where the scientific objective is rarely just to sample from the pre-trained distribution. Instead, a practitioner usually wants sequences with high activity, specificity, or other task-level scores for sequence design. Reward adaptation creates a tension between performance, generality, and cost. Training-based approaches can improve reward optimization, but they update the backbone and often require reward gradients, extra training, and hyperparameter tuning [ 8 , 9 ] . Training-free methods keep the backbone fixed, but many either assume differentiable rewards or rely on particle and search procedures whose cost grows with trajectory history or search width [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] . This motivates the question studied here: can a frozen masked diffusion model be adapted to generic black-box rewards by modifying only its inference-time sampling law? Our starting point is to view adaptation as a distributional transport problem. Let p θ p_{\theta} be the clean-sequence distribution induced by the frozen masked diffusion reverse chain, and let R : 𝒳 → ℝ R:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} be a sequence-level reward. Rather than optimizing reward in isolation, we target the reward-tilted distribution π β ​ ( 𝐱 ) ∝ p θ ​ ( 𝐱 ) ​ exp ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) / β ) \pi_{\beta}(\mathbf{x})\propto p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\exp(R(\bx)/\beta) , which keeps the pre-trained model as a sequence prior while favoring high-reward outputs. Doob’s h h -transform gives the exact local transformation needed to sample from this tilted law. The central object is the downstream value h ⁡ ( 𝐱 ¯ t l , t l ) h(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}},t_{l}) , the expected terminal reward weight under the frozen reverse chain conditioned on the current partially denoised state. The discrete setting changes how the transform must be implemented. In continuous diffusion, Doob guidance can be expressed as an additive score or drift correction [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] . In masked discrete diffusion, the state space is categorical, generation proceeds through irreversible token-reveal transitions, and there is no Euclidean score field. D-DOIT therefore applies Doob’s h h -transform at the kernel level: each frozen reverse transition is multiplicatively reweighted by the downstream h h -value of the candidate next state. This yields a discrete analogue of the continuous Doob correction while preserving the frozen parameters and allowing black-box reward queries. The exact transform still requires the future reward-to-go for every candidate reverse state, which is intractable by repeated rollouts. D-DOIT makes the transform executable with two approximations. First, it estimates candidate h h -values by using the masked diffusion prediction head to complete each candidate into a clean sequence, then evaluating the reward oracle on that completion. Second, it draws a finite set of candidate reverse states and selects among them with Doob-weighted probabilities. An optional best-of- K K refinement branches only after a chosen split update, which hedges irreversible token reveals without multiplying the full denoising trajectory cost. The same sampler gives two operating points: D-DOIT-LBOK-S for a lower-budget regime and D-DOIT-Q for high-budget quality evidence. We evaluate D-DOIT on regulatory DNA sequence design and protein inverse folding. On the DRAKES HepG2 enhancer benchmark, the near-TDS-speed D-DOIT-LBOK-S matches TDS on predicted activity while substantially improving accessibility, 3-mer correlation, and motif correlation. The high-budget D-DOIT-Q setting reaches 6.19 6.19 predicted activity and exceeds training-based DRAKES on Pred-Activity, 3-mer Corr, and JASPAR Corr, while remaining slightly lower on ATAC-Acc. At a similar wall-clock budget, D-DOIT-Q also improves activity, accessibility, and 3-mer correlation over soft value-based decoding (SVDD-PM) and wall-clock-matched endpoint search. Endpoint search achieves higher JASPAR correlation. On the Ctrl-DNA cell-type-specific enhancer benchmark, D-DOIT is a clear training-free method that moves the specificity reward. D-DOIT-Q raises Δ ​ R \Delta R to 0.119 0.119 , with a trade-off in motif preservation, and D-DOIT-LBOK-S provides a lower-budget positive-reward point. At a matched wall-clock budget, however, endpoint search captures much of this gain, so the margin is smaller than on HepG2. Guidance with alternative predictors and transfer to held-out evaluators retain the gains over unguided sampling. On protein inverse folding, the same frozen backbone reaches 68.1 % 68.1\% joint stability–structure success. These results support D-DOIT as a training-free mechanism for reward-guided sequence generation, not as a matched-cost replacement for every high-budget or training-based method. In summary, we make three contributions: • Discrete Doob h h -transform for masked diffusion. We formulate reward adaptation as sampling from a reward-tilted target distribution and derive the corresponding Doob h h -transform of the masked discrete diffusion reverse kernel. The resulting guidance reweights categorical token-reveal transitions, in contrast to the additive drift or score correction used in continuous diffusion. The exact reference transform is kept separate from the executable approximations built on it. • Executable finite-candidate sampler. We make the exact transform practical with a prediction-head h h -estimator, finite-candidate Doob-weighted selection, and an optional best-of- K K refinement for irreversible reveal decisions. The method uses only reward values and does not update the diffusion backbone. We characterize how tempering, sharpening, and terminal selection deviate from the exact target. • Biological validation and trade-offs. We test the same frozen-backbone sampler on HepG2 enhancer design, cell-type-specific enhancer design, and protein inverse folding. D-DOIT improves over training-free baselines across the reported reward-guided design tasks, while preserving the relevant trade-offs in naturalness, motif structure, and inference budget.

sections.heading: Organization.
sections.text: Section 2 reviews the masked discrete diffusion backbone, defines the reward-tilted target, and states the exact discrete Doob h h -transform. Section 3 develops the practical D-DOIT sampler, including the prediction-head h h -estimator, finite-candidate weighted update, and optional best-of- K K refinement. Section 4 reports experiments on regulatory DNA design, cell-type-specific enhancer design, and protein inverse folding. The appendix provides related work ( Appendix A ), the proof of the discrete Doob h h -transform ( Appendix B ), the standard masked diffusion sampler ( Appendix E ), and full experimental details ( Appendices J , K and M ).

sections.heading: 2 Preliminaries
sections.text: We first define the frozen masked diffusion reverse chain that serves as the base law for D-DOIT. We then state the reward-tilted target distribution and the discrete Doob h h -transform that transports this base law to the target without changing the model parameters [ 22 , 23 ] . We keep the exact reference transform separate from the executable approximation built on it, which Section 3 develops.

sections.heading: 3 D-DOIT: A Discrete Sampler Based on Doob’s h h -transform
sections.text: In this section, we introduce D-DOIT , a training-free sampler that guides a frozen masked discrete diffusion model toward the reward-tilted target in ( 2.3 ) using black-box rewards R : 𝒳 → ℝ R:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} defined on clean sequences. The exact transform in Theorem 2.1 says what the sampler should do: reweight each frozen reverse kernel by the downstream value ratio of the discrete Doob h h -function. The challenge is computational, since evaluating this value exactly would require future denoising rollouts from every candidate next state. D-DOIT therefore follows an exact-object-to-estimator design: it estimates the downstream value with the frozen prediction head, approximates the transformed kernel with finite candidates, and optionally branches late to hedge irreversible token reveals. Figure 1 summarizes the construction. Figure 1: Overview of D-DOIT. Left: Standard masked diffusion unmasks positions independently at each reverse step ( 2.1 ); it is cheap but reward-unaware. Right: One guided step approximately tilts the reverse kernel: it draws M = 3 M{=}3 candidates from a tempered proposal ( 3.6 ), completes and scores them with the prediction head and reward to obtain proxy h h -values, and selects the next state with sharpened h h -weights ( 3.7 ). Bottom: Optional best-of- K K refinement duplicates each trajectory into K = 4 K{=}4 copies after the split and keeps the highest-reward suffix ( 3.9 ), sharing prefix computation. Revealed tokens stay fixed; the practical sampler does not inherit the exact-target guarantee.

sections.heading: 3.1 D-DOIT Algorithm
sections.text: The transformed kernel in ( 2.5 ) depends on the downstream value h ⁡ ( 𝐲 ¯ t l − 1 , t l − 1 ) h(\bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}},t_{l-1}) for each candidate reverse state 𝐲 ¯ t l − 1 ∈ 𝒳 ~ \bar{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{l-1}}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{X}} reachable from the current state 𝐱 ¯ t l \bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}} . This subsection turns that exact identity into an executable sampler. The first component estimates each candidate’s downstream value with a prediction-head completion. The second component uses these values to form a finite-candidate approximation to the transformed kernel. The final component adds an optional best-of- K K refinement for the irreversible reveal structure of masked diffusion.

sections.text: A crucial aspect of estimating h h is how to obtain 𝐱 ^ 0 \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} ; while a common approach to maintaining speed is to estimate 𝐱 ^ 0 \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} directly from x t x_{t} in a single step, a more refined method involves obtaining 𝐱 ^ 0 \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} through iterative steps starting from x t x_{t} . Increasing completions per candidate from n h = 1 n_{h}=1 to 2 2 and 3 3 raises final guidance reward R R from 5.272 ± 0.057 5.272\pm 0.057 to 5.764 ± 0.033 5.764\pm 0.033 and 5.978 ± 0.026 5.978\pm 0.026 , at 41 % 41\% and 81 % 81\% additional wall time; we retain n h = 1 n_{h}=1 as the default. sections.heading: 4.6 Oracle Robustness
sections.text: The choice of reward function is independent of the D-DOIT algorithm itself, yet it significantly influences the algorithm’s performance. A more accurate reward function provides better guidance for the D-DOIT algorithm. To examine this, we designed various reward functions and observed their guiding effects. Replacing R R with Enformer, CNN, or MLP predictions improves all four metrics over unguided sampling ( Table 8 ); Pred-Activity reaches 4.491 4.491 , 2.203 2.203 , and 1.544 1.544 , versus 0.371 0.371 for the frozen model. Held-out rescoring preserves these gains ( Table 9 ), while evaluator scales remain incomparable. The controls support robustness across tested predictors without establishing experimental biological activity and are distinct from the high-budget 6.19 ± 0.05 6.19\pm 0.05 result.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion and Discussion
sections.text: We introduced D-DOIT, a training-free sampler that applies Doob’s h h -transform directly to frozen masked discrete diffusion models. Using a prediction-head h h -estimator and finite-candidate Doob-weighted selection, D-DOIT supports black-box rewards without reward gradients or backbone retraining. Across DRAKES HepG2, Ctrl-DNA, and protein inverse folding, D-DOIT outperforms training-free guidance baselines, although its highest-quality results require a larger compute budget. The method has three main limitations. First, practical approximations, including temperature scaling, sharpening, and best-of- K K selection, may introduce bias and do not retain the exact-target guarantee; late branching also cannot revise revealed tokens. Second, evaluation relies on predictive biological benchmarks and requires experimental validation. Third, the highest-quality setting incurs substantial recurring inference cost, leaving the reward–compute trade-off as a practical challenge. Overall, Doob-style kernel reweighting provides a general framework for guiding discrete generative models with sequence-level rewards.

sections.heading: Appendix A Related Work
sections.text: We review related work on reward-guided adaptation of discrete diffusion and flow models, as well as regulatory DNA sequence design.

sections.heading: Reward-guided adaptation of discrete diffusion and flow models.
sections.text: Reward-guided generation has proved effective for aligning language models [ 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 ] and diffusion models [ 33 , 34 , 35 ] with task-specific objectives. In discrete generative models, however, guidance must act on categorical transitions over a finite vocabulary. Early discrete denoising diffusion models use structured categorical or absorbing-state corruption [ 1 , 36 , 2 ] ; masked discrete diffusion models scale a simple absorbing-mask objective [ 3 , 4 ] ; score-entropy and ratio-matching parameterizations form a non-masked alternative [ 5 , 37 ] ; and discrete flow matching extends the same idea to a flow framework [ 38 , 39 ] . Reward adaptation for these models can be training-based or training-free. Training-based methods include DRAKES, which finetunes the generator through reward backpropagation [ 8 ] , trajectory-level alignment [ 9 ] , and reinforcement learning (RL)-style finetuning methods developed for continuous diffusion [ 40 , 41 , 42 , 43 ] ; these methods change backbone weights and need a differentiable reward. Training-free methods instead steer a frozen backbone at inference time, including Sequential Monte Carlo and twisted sampling [ 11 , 44 , 45 ] , posterior sampling for inverse problems [ 46 ] , soft value-based decoding [ 12 ] , reward-guided iterative refinement [ 13 ] , clean-sample Markov chains [ 47 ] , simple guidance for masked discrete diffusion [ 14 ] , denoising posterior prediction [ 15 ] , plug-and-play control [ 16 ] , and inference-time scaling [ 17 , 48 ] . These methods steer a frozen backbone, but they do not directly tilt the discrete reverse kernel toward an optimal proposal. Comparing with three representative efforts highlights the distinct role of D-DOIT. DRAKES [ 8 ] provides a strong reward-optimization baseline, but it finetunes the backbone and requires a differentiable reward. Soft value-based decoding [ 12 ] selects candidates using importance scores on intermediate latents, but it does not tilt the reverse transition kernel itself. Simple masked-diffusion guidance [ 14 ] introduces a heuristic guidance term, but lacks an explicit optimality target. In contrast, D-DOIT is the first inference-time method to implement an executable estimator of Doob’s h h -transform for the discrete reverse kernel [ 49 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 50 ] . It scores candidates through the resulting h h -tilted kernel, combines a frozen masked discrete diffusion backbone with a black-box reward, and further supports optional best-of- K K refinement over the same frozen prior. Because finite-candidate value-weighted selection also appears in soft value-based decoding and related methods, we do not claim that local candidate selection is unique to D-DOIT. CDM [ 51 ] learns a twist to amortize value estimation, and DPRM [ 52 ] applies Doob-derived corrections to token ordering while retaining a host token sampler; CSMC [ 47 ] instead searches over clean samples. Our distinction is the explicit categorical reverse-kernel h h -transform as the reference object, evaluated with a frozen prediction-head proxy rather than a learned value network.

sections.heading: Regulatory DNA sequence design.
sections.text: Regulatory DNA design aims to generate sequences that score well under predictive assays and stay faithful to natural regulatory grammar. Oracle-guided optimization with experimental validation drives early machine-guided enhancer design [ 53 , 24 , 54 ] ; autoregressive regulatory language models [ 26 ] and genomic foundation models [ 55 , 56 , 57 , 58 , 59 , 60 ] provide strong sequence priors; and diffusion-based generators specialize these priors through Dirichlet diffusion and score-entropy variants [ 6 , 7 , 61 ] . For reward-optimization benchmarks, DRAKES evaluates HepG2 enhancer generation through activity, accessibility, k k -mer, and motif-structure metrics [ 8 ] ; Ctrl-DNA studies cell-type-specific enhancer design through constrained reinforcement learning [ 25 ] ; and concurrent work combines discrete diffusion with tree search for cell-type-specific regulatory DNA design under related biological reward objectives [ 62 ] . The strongest methods on these benchmarks share one limit: they reach high reward only through backbone updates, policy training, or expanded inference search. Comparing with three representative efforts highlights the efficiency and generality of D-DOIT. DRAKES [ 8 ] finetunes the backbone and requires a differentiable reward. Ctrl-DNA [ 25 ] achieves cell-type specificity through constrained RL with reward signals shaped for policy optimization. The concurrent tree-search method of Awasthi et al. [62] remains training-free at inference time, but expands a search tree over partial sequences and increases the per-step sampling cost. In contrast, D-DOIT is the first method to compete on both benchmarks without policy training. It trades modest inference-time compute for reward gains while preserving near-base per-step cost.

sections.heading: Evaluation metrics.
sections.text: We use four metrics that cover predicted activity, chromatin accessibility, and sequence naturalness: • Predicted activity (Pred-Activity): We use the held-out evaluation reward oracle of [ 8 ] to estimate HepG2 enhancer activity for each generated sequence and report the median across the batch following the DRAKES convention. Higher scores indicate more functional sequences. • Chromatin accessibility (ATAC-Acc): We use an independent binary classifier trained on ENCODE HepG2 chromatin accessibility data [ 65 ] to test whether the designed sequences fall in accessible chromatin regions. This is a key property of active enhancers. Higher accuracy indicates more active sequences. • 3-mer pearson correlation (3-mer Corr): We compute the Pearson correlation between the 3 3 -mer frequency profile of the generated sequences and that of natural HepG2 enhancers from [ 24 ] . Higher correlation indicates that the generated sequences match the overall distribution of natural enhancer sequences. • JASPAR motif correlation (JASPAR Corr): We compute the Spearman correlation between the transcription-factor binding motif frequencies of the generated sequences and the natural enhancer reference, scored against the JASPAR motif database [ 66 ] . Higher correlation indicates better preservation of regulatory motif structure.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare D-DOIT against training-free and training-based methods. Training-free methods steer a frozen pre-trained model at inference time: • Pre-trained: the unguided masked discrete diffusion model of [ 8 ] ; provides the unguided reward and naturalness reference. • CG [ 10 ] : classifier guidance with discrete gradients; backpropagates through a Gumbel-Softmax relaxation and requires a differentiable reward. • SMC and TDS [ 11 ] : particle-based guidance with path likelihood ratios. TDS is a strong reported training-free baseline and provides the runtime reference for LBOK-S; its budget is not matched to Q. • SVDD-PM [ 12 ] : posterior-mean value decoding, using the same frozen MDLM and oracle protocol, with M = 416 M=416 for similar runtime to Q. • Frozen Best-of- N BoN N_{\mathrm{BoN}} : endpoint-only selection over independent unguided samples; N BoN = 732 N_{\mathrm{BoN}}=732 in the Q wall-clock comparison. Training-based methods update model parameters: • DRAKES [ 8 ] : reward finetunes the pre-trained masked discrete diffusion model with a KL regularizer; we treat it as the strongest naturalness-preserving training-based reference. • DRAKES w/o KL : removes the KL term to expose the over-optimization risk of unregularized reward maximization. • CFG [ 67 ] : trains a conditional model from scratch.

sections.heading: J.5 Additional Experimental Analysis
sections.text: For the experimental results in Table 2 , we provide the additional detailed analysis below. Section 4.1 reports the headline TDS comparisons. We add two pieces of detail here. First, the D-DOIT-LBOK-S vs. TDS gap on ATAC-Acc is + 25.0 +25.0 percentage points ( 40.0 % → 65.0 % 40.0\%\to 65.0\% ), while Pred-Activity is matched ( 4.56 4.56 vs. 4.58 4.58 ) with lower reported seed variability; this is descriptive, not a variance-test result. The same operating point also lifts ATAC-Acc from 39.9 % 39.9\% to 65.0 % 65.0\% over SMC and JASPAR Corr from 0.756 0.756 to 0.948 0.948 over SMC. Second, high-budget D-DOIT-Q over TDS gives + 1.61 +1.61 in Pred-Activity, + 51.7 +51.7 percentage points in ATAC-Acc, + 0.077 +0.077 in 3-mer Corr, and + 0.124 +0.124 in JASPAR Corr. Compared with the training-based DRAKES, D-DOIT-Q achieves higher Pred-Activity ( 6.19 6.19 vs. 5.61 5.61 ), higher 3-mer Corr ( 0.894 0.894 vs. 0.887 0.887 ), and higher JASPAR Corr ( 0.923 0.923 vs. 0.911 0.911 ) without any backbone update. DRAKES remains higher on ATAC-Acc ( 92.5 % 92.5\% vs. 91.7 % 91.7\% ), so we do not claim an all-metric win. The unregularized variant DRAKES w/o KL exposes the cost of training-based reward maximization: it gains + 0.83 +0.83 in Pred-Activity over DRAKES but loses 0.580 0.580 in 3-mer Corr ( 0.887 → 0.307 0.887\to 0.307 ) and 0.354 0.354 in JASPAR Corr ( 0.911 → 0.557 0.911\to 0.557 ). D-DOIT-Q stays near the DRAKES high-naturalness regime. The frozen model supplies candidate proposals without retraining. The exact reference transform reweights its induced distribution; the practical sampler’s temperatures and selection operations change that reference law. Figure 2 plots utility and naturalness for the original benchmark comparison set. The separately time-calibrated SVDD and endpoint controls are reported in Table 6 , rather than pooled into a claim of an exhaustive compute–quality frontier. D-DOIT-LBOK-S anchors the practical moderate-budget side of this frontier. D-DOIT-Q occupies the high-utility, high-naturalness corner when inference-time budget is deliberately relaxed, with ATAC-Acc as the remaining gap to DRAKES.

sections.heading: Appendix K Experimental Details of Cell-type-specific Enhancer Design
sections.text: In this section, we provide the experimental details and additional experimental analysis for the cell-type-specific enhancer design task in Section 4.2 .

sections.heading: Dataset.
sections.text: We use the 200 200 bp human enhancer corpus of Chen et al. [25] , covering three cell lines: HepG2, K562, and SK-N-SH. Data preprocessing follows the regLM protocol of Lal et al. [26] , as in Chen et al. [25] . We use the Ctrl-DNA enhancer task only for its data, cell-type-specific reward oracles, and evaluation metrics. The training procedure and backbone architecture come from our own setup, which we describe in the next paragraphs.

sections.heading: Reward oracle setup.

sections.text: We train a new masked discrete diffusion model [ 3 ] on the Ctrl-DNA enhancer corpus. The HyenaDNA backbone used by Chen et al. sections.heading: Evaluation metrics.
sections.text: We use three metrics that cover cell-type specificity, motif structure, and set-level diversity: • Cell-specific reward difference ( Δ ​ R \Delta R ): We compute the difference between the target-cell oracle score and the average of the off-target oracle scores following the Ctrl-DNA convention. Higher scores indicate stronger cell-type specificity. • Motif correlation (Motif Corr): We compute the Pearson correlation between the transcription-factor binding-site frequencies of the generated sequences and the cell-type-specific natural enhancer set from [ 25 ] (top half by target activity, bottom half by off-target activity). Higher correlation indicates that the generated sequences match the regulatory grammar of natural cell-specific enhancers. • Set-level diversity (Diversity): We compute the Shannon entropy across the generated sequence set with the official Ctrl-DNA evaluation script [ 25 ] . Higher entropy indicates that the sampler does not collapse onto a small set of high-reward sequences. Δ ​ R \Delta R and Motif Corr appear in Table 3 . Diversity appears in Figure 3 . We omit Median because [ 25 ] mentions it in text but does not report numerical values.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare D-DOIT against the baselines from Chen et al. [25] and the same training-free guidance methods as in Section J.2 : • Pre-trained , CG [ 10 ] , SMC , TDS [ 11 ] : training-free inference-time methods on the same frozen masked discrete diffusion model. These share the frozen backbone with D-DOIT. Frozen Best-of-708 additionally provides the same-A100 endpoint-search control at Q’s measured time budget. • regLM [ 26 ] : supervised generative baseline that the authors train on the cell-type-specific enhancer corpus. • PPO, TACO, PPO-Lagrangian [ 25 ] : RL-based methods that retrain the generator against the specificity reward. • AdaLead, PEX, BO, CMA-ES [ 25 ] : directed-evolution methods that search the sequence space directly without any generative backbone.

sections.heading: Appendix L Ablation Study
sections.text: We conduct ablation studies on the DRAKES HepG2 enhancer task to understand the behavior of D-DOIT. We examine the guidance window l ∗ l^{*} , guidance strength ω \omega and effective sample size (ESS), proposal and completion temperatures τ , γ \tau,\gamma , and candidate budget M M . We also study completion count, direct-versus-rollout value estimates, soft-versus-argmax selection, split position, and reward trajectories ( Tables 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 and 21 ). The window, strength, temperature, and candidate-budget sweeps use a single held-out seed unless noted otherwise; the additional diagnostics state their sampling protocols separately. Final guidance reward R R is scored by the sampling oracle and is distinct from held-out Pred-Activity. Completion-proxy trajectories use the held-out evaluator but average scores of completed partial states rather than the benchmark’s within-seed batch median. We re-run the best γ \gamma -sweep configuration across the 3 3 main evaluation seeds and report it in Table 15 . These studies show how D-DOIT balances reward optimization, sequence naturalness, and computational cost. The candidate-budget sweep shows that increasing M M mainly improves functional utility, while naturalness metrics remain comparatively stable. The table surfaces three consequential design choices: the guidance window l ∗ l^{*} exhibits a phase transition for naturalness; the completion temperature γ \gamma controls prediction-head completion quality; and the candidate budget M M controls utility. sections.heading: Runtime analysis.
sections.text: Section 4.4 reports the runtime comparison and its measurement conditions. The runtime pattern follows the NFE accounting in Appendix G : larger M M and earlier best-of- K K splitting increase candidate-state evaluations and oracle-scored completions. Increasing n h n_{h} also increases completion scoring, as quantified in Table 16 . LBOK-S is the lower-budget operating point, whereas Q deliberately trades greater recurring inference cost for quality; neither setting implies cost dominance over training-based methods.

sections.heading: L.1 Effect of Guidance Window l ∗ l^{*}
sections.text: Figure 4: Guidance-window sweep. Expanding the guided window improves utility and sharply recovers naturalness between l ∗ = 96 l^{*}=96 and l ∗ = 112 l^{*}=112 . We study the effect of the guidance window l ∗ l^{*} , the highest reverse-time index where Doob’s h h -transform is active in the discrete sampler. A smaller l ∗ l^{*} saves ( L − l ∗ ) ⋅ M (L-l^{*})\cdot M neural-function evaluations per sequence but omits guidance at more heavily masked states, where limited revealed context may affect the prediction-head proxy. Figure 4 reports the four DRAKES metrics as we sweep l ∗ ∈ { 10 , 20 , … , 128 } l^{*}\in\{10,20,\ldots,128\} . The results show a phase-transition-like behavior in naturalness. All configurations with l ∗ ≤ 50 l^{*}\leq 50 produce negative 3-mer Pearson correlations. A sharp jump occurs between l ∗ = 96 l^{*}{=}96 (3-mer = 0.21 =0.21 ) and l ∗ = 112 l^{*}{=}112 ( 0.65 0.65 ). At l ∗ = 128 l^{*}{=}128 , 3-mer reaches 0.894 0.894 , a 14 × 14\times improvement over l ∗ = 64 l^{*}{=}64 . Utility metrics improve across the same range without a sharp transition. In this sweep, broad guidance windows are associated with better global sequence-composition statistics; this observation does not isolate a causal mechanism or establish a requirement for other rewards. Utility metrics, in contrast, recover from a narrower window. We use l ∗ = 128 l^{*}{=}128 as the default setting.

sections.heading: L.2 Effect of Guidance Strength ω \omega and ESS Collapse
sections.text: We study the effect of the guidance strength ω \omega in ( 3.7 ). A larger ω \omega sharpens the transformed transition toward high-reward candidates. A smaller ω \omega preserves more of the pre-trained kernel. Figure 5: ESS diagnostic. ESS and collapse fraction across ω \omega ; weighted selection collapses to near-greedy at ω ≥ 4 \omega\geq 4 . Figure 5 reports the per-step Effective Sample Size (ESS) of the candidate weights and the fraction of steps where ESS collapses below M / 4 M/4 . The results show that ESS collapses to near 1 1 at ω ≥ 4 \omega\geq 4 . 95 % 95\% of guided steps have ESS < M / 4 <M/4 at ω = 4 \omega{=}4 , and 100 % 100\% at ω ≥ 16 \omega\geq 16 . A direct mechanism for concentration is reward-range amplification: ω = 4 \omega{=}4 amplifies a candidate reward range of ≈ 3 \approx 3 nats to ≥ 12 \geq 12 nats and saturates the softmax. High-quality results remain achievable despite this collapse when proposal-level diversity (via τ \tau ) still places a strong candidate in the pool. This motivates joint tuning of ω \omega and τ \tau , but does not imply that larger τ \tau recovers importance-weight accuracy. The concentration depends on the reward distribution and ω / β \omega/\beta , so these diagnostic thresholds cannot be transferred unchanged to other configurations.

sections.heading: L.3 Effect of Proposal and Completion Temperatures τ , γ \tau,\gamma
sections.text: We then study the joint effect of the proposal temperature τ \tau in ( 3.6 ) and the completion temperature γ \gamma in ( 3.3 ). A larger τ \tau flattens the proposal and produces more diverse candidates. A smaller γ \gamma sharpens the prediction-head completion toward the model mode. Figure 6 reports the four DRAKES metrics across the joint sweep at M = 32 M{=}32 . The results show a clear separation of roles. Functional activity peaks at higher proposal diversity. Marginal analysis shows Pred-Activity improves from 3.89 3.89 at τ = 2.5 \tau{=}2.5 to 4.07 4.07 at τ = 5.0 \tau{=}5.0 , and ATAC-Acc from 53.7 % 53.7\% to 69.4 % 69.4\% . Naturalness peaks at sharper prediction-head completions. Reducing γ \gamma from 1.2 1.2 to 0.6 0.6 improves averaged 3-mer Corr from 0.846 0.846 to 0.905 0.905 . At the strongest γ \gamma -sweep configuration ( M = 32 M{=}32 , τ = 3.0 \tau{=}3.0 , γ = 0.6 \gamma{=}0.6 ), 3-mer Corr reaches 0.949 ± 0.006 0.949\pm 0.006 across 3 3 seeds, above DRAKES at 0.887 0.887 . This sweep identifies the naturalness-preserving region. The final held-out DRAKES Q row in Table 2 uses a larger eval-selected inference budget and trades some naturalness for much higher Pred-Activity and ATAC-Acc while remaining above the DRAKES 3-mer and JASPAR targets. Naturalness metrics saturate around τ = 3.5 \tau{=}3.5 – 4.0 4.0 , suggesting a trade-off between naturalness and accessibility at extreme proposal temperatures. We use τ = 3.0 \tau{=}3.0 and γ = 0.6 \gamma{=}0.6 as the ablation default for naturalness-preserving sweeps. Figure 6: Interaction of proposal and completion temperatures. We sweep the proposal temperature τ \tau and the completion temperature γ \gamma at M = 32 M=32 . Naturalness peaks at sharper prediction-head completions (smaller γ \gamma ), while functional activity peaks at higher proposal diversity (larger τ \tau ). sections.heading: L.4 Effect of Candidate Budget M M
sections.text: We study the effect of the Monte Carlo candidate budget M M . The candidate count controls per-step work and coverage of possible next states. This sweep measures quality changes, not kernel error or convergence to the original tilted distribution. Figure 7 reports the four DRAKES metrics across M ∈ { 8 , 16 , 32 } M\in\{8,16,32\} . Figure 7: Candidate-budget sweep. We vary the Monte Carlo candidate budget M M on the DRAKES HepG2 task and report the same four metrics. Increasing M M gives direct gains in functional utility, while naturalness changes much less across the sweep. The results show that fewer candidates reduce functional utility but leave sequence naturalness almost unchanged. Reducing M M from 32 32 to 8 8 drops Pred-Activity by 31 % 31\% and ATAC-Acc by 29 % 29\% . 3-mer Corr drops by 9 % 9\% and JASPAR Corr by less than 1 % 1\% . The temperatures and the guidance window drive naturalness. A larger candidate count gives more direct help to utility. M = 32 M{=}32 provides a strong per-step default within the ablation sweep. The final held-out DRAKES Q row uses a larger budget, M = 52 M{=}52 with K = 8 K{=}8 , for the no-budget-limit quality comparison in Table 2 .

Abstract We propose D-DOIT (Discrete Doob-Oriented Inference-time Transformation), a training-free and efficient adaptation method for discrete diffusion models with generic rewards. D-DOIT formulates adaptation as sampling from a reward-tilted target distribution and realizes this transport through Doob’s h h -transform of the discrete diffusion reverse kernel, using only reward values rather than reward gradients. Unlike continuous diffusion, masked discrete diffusion samples categorical token-reveal transitions rather than continuous state updates. D-DOIT derives the corresponding discrete Doob’s h h -transform, which guides sampling by reweighting reverse transition probabilities instead of adding a drift correction. To make this transformation practical, D-DOIT avoids expensive future rollouts. At each guided step, D-DOIT samples candidate next states, uses the model prediction head to complete each candidate into a clean sequence, evaluates each completion with the reward oracle, and resamples the next state with probabilities proportional to the rewards. An optional late-stage best-of- K K refinement further improves sample quality by branching trajectories only near the end of denoising, avoiding the K K -fold cost over the full trajectory. Empirically, across regulatory DNA design and protein inverse folding benchmarks, D-DOIT outperforms training-free guidance baselines. It improves enhancer activity and cell-type specificity while preserving sequence naturalness, and achieves the highest success rate in protein inverse folding. Project Page: https://github.com/WeiminWu2000/D-DOIT . 1 Introduction We propose D-DOIT ( D iscrete D oob- O riented I nference-time T ransformation), a training-free sampler for reward-guided masked discrete diffusion. Discrete diffusion has become a strong generative modeling paradigm for finite-vocabulary data [ 1 , 2 ] . Masked discrete diffusion models are especially attractive for biological sequences because they predict clean tokens from partially masked states and provide tractable categorical reverse kernels [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . These models have recently been used for DNA and protein generation [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] , where the scientific objective is rarely just to sample from the pre-trained distribution. Instead, a practitioner usually wants sequences with high activity, specificity, or other task-level scores for sequence design. Reward adaptation creates a tension between performance, generality, and cost. Training-based approaches can improve reward optimization, but they update the backbone and often require reward gradients, extra training, and hyperparameter tuning [ 8 , 9 ] . Training-free methods keep the backbone fixed, but many either assume differentiable rewards or rely on particle and search procedures whose cost grows with trajectory history or search width [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] . This motivates the question studied here: can a frozen masked diffusion model be adapted to generic black-box rewards by modifying only its inference-time sampling law? Our starting point is to view adaptation as a distributional transport problem. Let p θ p_{\theta} be the clean-sequence distribution induced by the frozen masked diffusion reverse chain, and let R : 𝒳 → ℝ R:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} be a sequence-level reward. Rather than optimizing reward in isolation, we target the reward-tilted distribution π β ​ ( 𝐱 ) ∝ p θ ​ ( 𝐱 ) ​ exp ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) / β ) \pi_{\beta}(\mathbf{x})\propto p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\exp(R(\bx)/\beta) , which keeps the pre-trained model as a sequence prior while favoring high-reward outputs. Doob’s h h -transform gives the exact local transformation needed to sample from this tilted law. The central object is the downstream value h ⁡ ( 𝐱 ¯ t l , t l ) h(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{l}},t_{l}) , the expected terminal reward weight under the frozen reverse chain conditioned on the current partially denoised state. The discrete setting changes how the transform must be implemented. In continuous diffusion, Doob guidance can be expressed as an additive score or drift correction [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] . In masked discrete diffusion, the state space is categorical, generation proceeds through irreversible token-reveal transitions, and there is no Euclidean score field. D-DOIT therefore applies Doob’s h h -transform at the kernel level: each frozen reverse transition is multiplicatively reweighted by the downstream h h -value of the candidate next state. This yields a discrete analogue of the continuous Doob correction while preserving the frozen parameters and allowing black-box reward queries. The exact transform still requires the future reward-to-go for every candidate reverse state, which is intractable by repeated rollouts. D-DOIT makes the transform executable with two approximations. First, it estimates candidate h h -values by using the masked diffusion prediction head to complete each candidate into a clean sequence, then evaluating the reward oracle on that completion. Second, it draws a finite set of candidate reverse states and selects among them with Doob-weighted probabilities. An optional best-of- K K refinement branches only after a chosen split update, which hedges irreversible token reveals without multiplying the full denoising trajectory cost. The same sampler gives two operating points: D-DOIT-LBOK-S for a lower-budget regime and D-DOIT-Q for high-budget quality evidence. We evaluate D-DOIT on regulatory DNA sequence design and protein inverse folding. On the DRAKES HepG2 enhancer benchmark, the near-TDS-speed D-DOIT-LBOK-S matches TDS on predicted activity while substantially improving accessibility, 3-mer correlation, and motif correlation. The high-budget D-DOIT-Q setting reaches 6.19 6.19 predicted activity and exceeds training-based DRAKES on Pred-Activity, 3-mer Corr, and JASPAR Corr, while remaining slightly lower on ATAC-Acc. At a similar wall-clock budget, D-DOIT-Q also improves activity, accessibility, and 3-mer correlation over soft value-based decoding (SVDD-PM) and wall-clock-matched endpoint search. Endpoint search achieves higher JASPAR correlation. On the Ctrl-DNA cell-type-specific enhancer benchmark, D-DOIT is a clear training-free method that moves the specificity reward. D-DOIT-Q raises Δ ​ R \Delta R to 0.119 0.119 , with a trade-off in motif preservation, and D-DOIT-LBOK-S provides a lower-budget positive-reward point. At a matched wall-clock budget, however, endpoint search captures much of this gain, so the margin is smaller than on HepG2. Guidance with alternative predictors and transfer to held-out evaluators retain the gains over unguided sampling. On protein inverse folding, the same frozen backbone reaches 68.1 % 68.1\% joint stability–structure success. These results support D-DOIT as a training-free mechanism for reward-guided sequence generation, not as a matched-cost replacement for every high-budget or training-based method. In summary, we make three contributions: • Discrete Doob h h -transform for masked diffusion. We formulate reward adaptation as sampling from a reward-tilted target distribution and derive the corresponding Doob h h -transform of the masked discrete diffusion reverse kernel. The resulting guidance reweights categorical token-reveal transitions, in contrast to the additive drift or score correction used in continuous diffusion. The exact reference transform is kept separate from the executable approximations built on it. • Executable finite-candidate sampler. We make the exact transform practical with a prediction-head h h -estimator, finite-candidate Doob-weighted selection, and an optional best-of- K K refinement for irreversible reveal decisions. The method uses only reward values and does not update the diffusion backbone. We characterize how tempering, sharpening, and terminal selection deviate from the exact target. • Biological validation and trade-offs. We test the same frozen-backbone sampler on HepG2 enhancer design, cell-type-specific enhancer design, and protein inverse folding. D-DOIT improves over training-free baselines across the reported reward-guided design tasks, while preserving the relevant trade-offs in naturalness, motif structure, and inference budget.
